name: Nothing After 1948
summary: Delhi, 31 January 1981: about 300,000 volunteers fill Rajpath for one take of the funeral in Gandhi, and you run Checkpoint 4 of Sector C. You turn each person from 1981 back into 1948: watches go into a ticking Dalda tin in exchange for brass tokens, sunglasses and nylon come off. Then you sort them FRONT, MIDDLE or BACK, hunt down a cricket radio, hand out marigold petals and stand silent at the rope as the gun carriage passes. Afterwards you give everyone their time back, your own watch last.
motifs: a tin full of ticking watches
a crowd in white to the horizon
marigold petals on a red road
a Polaroid developing in the sun
thread: The player followed the cable down and came out holding a gate on Rajpath, Delhi, on the morning in 1981 when Gandhi's funeral was restaged for the film. They took the time off everyone by putting all the watches in a tin, their own Casio first. They sorted a city's worth of white into front, middle and back, and let one watch stay: a 1946 Sowar that had been on that road the first time, worn by the daughter who stood on her father's shoulders. They stood silent while the carriage passed, one take, and then gave every watch back. Their own beeped 10:00 on their wrist. Mrs Arora looked at the boiler print and said: so it was found, then it's a grave too, be careful with it. Carried: the thermal print of the boiler (01:05), a Polaroid of Sector C's front row still coming up out of brown, and the Casio, keeping 1981 time. They picked up the end of the gun carriage's drag rope and followed it east down the empty road toward India Gate. Still open: once you've given a thing its proper send-off, what do you keep, and who is the picture for?
delight: My favourite thing is that to step into 1948, a third of a million people had to hand over 1981, and in this space it literally ticks in a ghee tin. You give out a brass token for each watch and get the time only from a loudhailer, until your own Casio beeps ten o'clock on your wrist. I loved Kamla's father's watch being the one thing you shouldn't sort out, because it was there the first time, and a bandmaster who shakes his Polaroid even though he knows it's a superstition.

idea.name: The Middle Watch
idea.premise: What you owe the things you wanted so badly to find: a wreck found at 2 a.m. in 1985, then a funeral restaged in the Delhi sun in 1981. Each space is a careful ritual of sorting and keeping time for the dead, and the thing passed from hand to hand changes each time: cable, rope, thermal print, Polaroid.
